newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Eritrean central banker says economy doing well.
newsitem.headline: Eritrean central banker says economy doing well.

text.p: Eritrea's chief banker said on Wednesday the Red Sea state was building an economy ruined by a 30-year liberation war and results so far were satisfactory.
Tekie Beyene, governor of the central National Bank of Eritrea, told Reuters in Addis Ababa that the economic performance of Africa's newest country was "very satisfactory".
Quoting International Monetary Fund (IMF) figures, Tekie said gross domestic product (GDP) grew at 6.8 percent in 1996 and forecast a rise in GDP growth in 1997.
He said inflation in Eritrea stood at 2.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and was expected to stay in that range. He did not give comparative figures for the previous year.
Tekie said he was quoting IMF figures because of a lack of reliable data in Eritrea, which became independent from Ethiopia in 1993.
Eritrea, with a population of about four million, still suffers from a lack of skilled manpower and is trying to build a working bureau of statistics, according to financial experts.
Tekie said programmes to upgrade its infrastructure were in progress and targets included the rehabilitation and construction of schools, hospitals, and water and electricity.
He did not say where the money for the rehabilitation was coming from but Eritrea is known among donors for being wary of undertaking large foreign-funded projects and relying on its own resources.
New roads were under construction and old ones were being repaired, Tekie said.

Eritrea was a province of Ethiopia until independence in May 1993. It fought a gruelling 30-year war for its freedom, which was ensured by the fall of Ethiopian Marxist dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam in 1991.
Eritrea called a referendum on independence under the supervision of the United Nations in 1991, leading to independence two years later under President Isayas Afewerki.

The Red Sea port of Massawa, which was virtually destroyed by an Ethiopian air strike during the war, as well as Assab which Ethiopia uses for imports and exports were being rehabilitated, Tekie said.
He did not give a cost for the rehabilitation projects.
Tekie said infratsructural development was being undertaken across the whole country "to satisfy the educational and health requirements of the Eritrean people".
He said Eritrea had listed 43 public enterprises and factories for sale in its privatisation drive.
"The privatisation agency has already distributed bid documents to interested buyers -- foreign as well as local investors," said Tekie.

He said the new Eritrean currency, the nakfa, was expected in circulation hopefully before the end of 1997. Eritrea still uses the Ethiopian birr as its currency at a rate of 6.643 to the dollar this week.
Nakfa is the name of a northern Eritrean town which was a key to the Eritrean guerrilla movement in the war with Ethiopia.
